articles.title: Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU
articles.summary: Amid global tumult, the two countries' alliance is not the only unlikely pairing.
articles.preview: On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times. Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce.
articles.body:
On the streets of Barcelona, fiery red and gold Chinese dragons (presumably with very sweaty people inside the costumes) danced among delighted crowds, while Chinese acrobats elicited gasps of amazement as they rolled, tossed and threw spherical lanterns in the air, keeping - as if by magic - the candle inside them upright at all times.

Shanghai made history this week: the first Asian metropolis to be invited as the city of honour to Barcelona's famously rambunctious cultural festival, La Merce. Vast street processions here are overwhelmingly aimed at celebrating centuries-old Catalan traditions. So it was quite something to witness velvet-clad Catalan pipers, sashaying down Barcelona's main boulevards, their medieval tunes intermingling with lilting music that accompanied flocks of brightly dressed Chinese performers.

Shanghai Vice Mayor Lu Shan flew to Barcelona to speak at La Merce's opening ceremony. Chinese and Catalan cultural traditions differ in form, he remarked, but they share "a common spirit".

Spain and China are experiencing a period of mutual appreciation. But that sense of bonhomie is far from shared across the EU.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez has visited China's President Xi Jinping four times in as many years. He's urged the EU as a whole to improve relations with China since Donald Trump's re-election two years ago.

Sanchez's move has sparked resentment and disapproval among a number of Spain's European partners who view Beijing as a strategic rival and possible geopolitical threat to the EU. Privately, they ask if Madrid's welcoming stance - opening up its market to Chinese businesses - is enabling China to become the (economic) enemy within the bloc too.

Pedro Sanchez is not the only EU leader going off piste. Global volatility means other EU countries feel squeezed and exposed and unsure they can rely on America under President Trump. His policy on trade and defence is seen as unpredictable and, at times, aggressive. And so EU member states are selecting strategic partners that they believe suit their national needs, even if that alienates or irritates fellow member states.

So do these new-found alliances risk a permanent splintering of unity in the EU or even Nato?

Spain accused of self-interest

Germany and France - the EU's biggest powers - have just united around a more aggressive approach towards China. They want to give Brussels the muscle to shut subsidised Chinese competitors out of the EU market to address ballooning trade imbalances with Beijing that the European Commission claims have reached a whopping â¬1bn (Â£850m) a day.

Other EU countries fret about China's tight relationship with Russia. Beijing has denied helping Moscow's war effort in Ukraine but defence experts point to technological and economic support from China, which they say has enabled Russia to sustain its military assault.

That's why, as Spain enthusiastically courts Beijing, it stands accused of looking after its own, rather than wider European interests.

"It's a bit chicken and egg. Did Spain distance itself from European allies, or did they distance themselves from us?" asks Victor Cortizo, a lawyer and academic specialising in Sino-Spanish relations.

"I think it's more us. It's Spain. But legitimately so. Realpolitik is a thing. If I get closer to China because that attracts Chinese investment and bolsters my economy, then that is strategically more appealing than supporting allies who are also only looking out for themselves."

Cortizo and I were surrounded by towers of crates as we spoke, at the end of the longest freight rail link in the world. It runs over 13,000km (8,000 miles) between Yiwu in eastern China and Madrid, largely bringing car parts and electrical goods to Spain and transporting delicacies like Spanish ham and red wine back to China. The link is a symbol of the burgeoning relations between the two countries.

"Our prime minister has made the decision to pursue national gain over EU relations," Cortizo told me. "Chinese investment in Spain has doubled over the last year alone."

Rising Chinese investment

According to ICEX Spain Trade and Investment, the Spanish government's trade and investment agency, Chinese investments in Spain are surging, driven in particular by investments in new battery gigafactories and car plants.

Cortizo thinks Spain could become Beijing's preferred European country to invest in now that Hungary is no longer governed by pro-China Viktor Orban, under whom Hungary was dubbed "China's gateway into Europe".

"US investment is sinking and Chinese investment [is] rising in relevance here," Cortizo told me.

The US remains Spain's largest single foreign investor but net investment was down by around â¬1bn, according to Spain's Economy Ministry.

Spanish society now has a far more favourable attitude towards China than towards the US, its traditional ally.

According to a Pew Research Center poll published this summer, 54% of Spaniards said they had a favourable opinion of China compared to 30% who viewed the US favourably.

China makes it easy to trade, Cortizo told me, while the US (through Trump's tariffs and the effects of the war in Iran) has made it far harder. Meanwhile, Spaniards have seen the US president threatening their prime minister with economic sanctions when he doesn't agree to Donald Trump's demands to increase defence spending to 5% of GDP or allow US bases in Spain to be used as part of attacks on Iran.

That's why China is viewed by many in Spain as more reliable than the US.

And when the major Chinese car manufacturer Chery Automobile chose Spain for its first European manufacturing and operations hub two years ago, it breathed life back into then-defunct Spanish brand Ebro.

"Chinese companies are investing in car manufacturing in Spain, filling the gaps we had," says Cortizo.

But critics worry Chinese factories on Spanish soil will weaken the EU single market.

There isn't just Chery in Barcelona. Chinese battery and stationary-energy-storage company Hithium plans to invest in Navarra in the north of Spain and battery manufacturer CATL is involved in building a lithium iron phosphate battery gigafactory in Zaragoza, 200 miles west of Barcelona. Critics fear these projects are part of Chinese companies' efforts to localise production in the EU to evade tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles.

However, Miguel Otero, China specialist at Madrid's ElCano Royal Institute, accuses Spain's European allies of being condescending and hypocritical.

"France, Italy, Germany, they all have their own strategic relationship with China," he tells me. "Spain isn't going much further. It's been catching up with them." In fact, he says, now that Europe can no longer rely fully on the US, Spain's priority is to diversify. It wants to do business not just with China but also Canada, Brazil, India and Africa. Spain is not China-obsessed, he says.

But there's also the question of security.

On his latest trip to Beijing in April, Prime Minister Sanchez met the founder of Chinese wind turbine manufacturer Ming Yang, which had just had its plans to open the UK's largest wind turbine manufacturing plant in the Highlands blocked on national security grounds.

This followed uproar in the EU after Spain's Ministry of the Interior awarded Chinese tech giant Huawei a â¬12.3m contract to store and manage sensitive judicial wiretap data last year.

MEPs from several political groups in the European Parliament said Spain's contract could endanger the EU as a whole.

"When you introduce a high-risk vendor... we do not just risk a localised data breach, we risk poisoning the well of European intelligence sharing," said Markéta Gregorová, a Czech Pirate Party MEP, part of the Greens group back in February.

Juan Ignacio Zoido Ãlvarez, a member of Spain's centre-right opposition party, said the decision puts "the entirety of the EU at risk".

Spain's defence ministry continues to deny there is any risk, but former US Ambassador to Nato Julianne Smith, the co-founder of geostrategic advisory firm Clarion Strategies, warns the episode could really erode European cohesion.

"As EU countries seek ways to hedge against what some see as an unpredictable and unreliable America, they have to be careful not to rush towards alternatives that stand to weaken the EU's collective hand," she tells me.

"Some of those growing relationships, such as Canada's rapidly expanding relationship with the EU, could produce real dividends," she added. "But others, such as Spain's decision to deepen its relationship with China, could further derail the EU's ability to speak with one voice and create added security vulnerabilities for both Spain and wider Europe."

More emerging alliances

Spain is far from alone amongst EU countries in striking up controversial alliances.

Finland has a massive 1,300km-long land border with Russia. This has left it feeling exposed since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Finland already has the highest rate of civilian firearm ownership per capita in the EU. It has the largest reserve military force in both the EU and Nato. It has built cavities under bridges that can be packed with explosives, should Russian armoured vehicles enter its territory. This is a country that believes military preparedness is an existential necessity.

In 2022, it decided there was safety in numbers. Helsinki ditched its traditional strategic neutrality and rushed to join Nato.

Now though, there are fears that Washington might not respect the alliance's mutual defence clause in case of an attack on a member country.

No longer confident the US would come to the rescue if needed, Finland has turned to Israel to purchase advanced defence equipment, including the David's Sling air-defence system and Spike anti-tank missiles.

Finland renewed its contract with Israel at the height of the recent Gaza war despite its government having publicly expressed considerable reservations about Israeli activity in the occupied Palestinian territories and at a time when many other EU countries also feel deep unease about Israel's policies and activities in Gaza and the West Bank.

"There is a sense in Finland that we can't always afford [to have] a moral superiority. Survival comes at a price," says Minna Alander, a fellow with the Transatlantic Defence and Security Programme at the Center for European Policy Analysis (CEPA).

"Finns and political opposition parties do question whether Israel is a country whose defence industry they want to support [because of its actions in Gaza and the West Bank] but the Finnish government has kept out of the debate, saying the deal with Israel fulfils Finland's needs," she tells me.

In the end, Alander says her fellow Finns have "a less sentimental mentality".

Greece's shift

Greece also feels threatened by a far bigger, immediate neighbour. It perceives Turkey as a "constant and significant danger to its national security and sovereignty", Nick Malkoutzis, co-founder of political analysis website MacroPolis, tells me.

In the past, the US mediated disputes between the two countries. Both are members of Nato. But under Donald Trump, Nato insiders say the US is increasingly perceived as missing in action politically and diplomatically, with Washington's focus very much elsewhere.

In late August, Greece and Israel signed one of the largest defence export deals in both countries' histories. The "Achilles Shield" agreement provides Athens with Israeli technology aimed at protecting Greece against a range of threats, including drones, aircraft and missiles.

There is a history of public sympathy with the Palestinian cause in Greece and many people have been sceptical about ever closer relations with Israel. But Malkoutsis says the public and political reaction to the "mega-deal" with Israel has been "more muted than might have been expected".

He says this is because there is a bottom line - a common understanding of the fundamental need for Greece to strengthen its security in relation to Turkey that takes priority over everything else.

With Israel a close ally of Washington, Greece hopes that "buying Israeli" will also help maintain decent relations with the US, even in these turbulent times.

But it's a delicate dance because Greece and Finland both very much want to be seen as "good Europeans", feeding into the European collective, according to Malkoutsis.

He says EU countries "scrambling in all directions" complicate everyone getting on the same page and speaking with one voice on defence and security which is the opposite of what Brussels and Nato say they want.

That said, European countries banding together in smaller groups to pursue common interests is nothing new. The E3 "gang", composed of the UK, Germany and France, was originally formed in 2003 to co-ordinate diplomatic negotiations with Iran in the hope of a nuclear deal. It's now a more ad hoc communication channel for Europe's three largest military and economic powers.

Nordic and Arctic nations have their own formats for working together to promote regional defence, while the "Visegrad Four" made up of Czechia, Hungary, Poland and Slovakia was for many years a well-known pressure group in EU circles.

However, Nato and the EU are convinced that the continent is under intense pressure, unprecedented since the end of the World War Two. Their leaders say it is time to form a united front. An aggressive Russia growls threateningly at the door, bolstered by Beijing, while the United States, Europe's former best friend abroad, seems, at best, distracted by other priorities.

Splintering, fracturing and rampant "mini-lateralism" will only be applauded by Europe's adversaries, they believe. China and Russia are watching closely.

articles.title: Legge elettorale al via alla Camera: la fiducia del governo e lo sciopero della fame di Magi
articles.summary: AGI - La legge elettorale torna alla Camera in terza lettura, con il governo che si prepara a porre tre fiducie su altrettanti articoli modificati a Palazzo Madama e Riccardo Magi che annuncia uno sciopero della fame contro quello che definisce "un colpo di stato elettorale che vuole consentire a una minoranza nel Paese di diventare maggioranza schiacciante in Parlamento". La legge elettorale e lo sciopero della fame Il leader di +Europa lancia la protesta durante una conferenza stampa, convocata ieri 30 settembre alla Camera. "Da oggi inizierò un digiuno per ottenere la modifica almeno delle parti peggiori di questa norma e consentire di presentare le liste con la firma digitale", dice. "Noi lotteremo fino all'ultimo per modificare questa legge e se non sarà modificata in Parlamento continueremo la battaglia nel paese attraverso i ricorsi in tribunale", assicura Magi. Che prepara, in parallelo, una serie di "iniziative non violente e ricorsi in sedi giurisdizionali" su cui +Europa "sta già lavorando". I nodi della protesta Al centro dei rilievi, condivisi dalle altre opposizioni, l'equa rappresentanza dei generi, perché "si travolge completamente l'equilibrio di genere nelle candidature" e la norma che introduce un tetto di firme più alto per chi si presenta alle elezioni per la prima volta. "Sono state aumentate a dismisura le firme necessarie per presentarsi alle elezioni. Di fatto sono necessarie 450.000 firme per una nuova forza politica che vuole cimentarsi con la democrazia elettorale. Una cosa incredibile e sicuramente incostituzionale", osserva il segretario di +Europa. La fase finale del percorso parlamentare del testo In parallelo alla protesta di stampo Radicale di Magi, entra nell'ultima fase il percorso parlamentare del testo, dopo che - a luglio scorso - la maggioranza era 'andata sotto', con il voto segreto, sull'emendamento che introduceva le preferenze, poi passate al Senato. La legge elettorale, ieri pomeriggio, è tornata in Aula alla Camera, dopo l'approvazione del testo e l'ok al mandato al relatore in commission e Affari Costituzionali . Oltre a quelli di maggioranza, ci saranno anche quattro relatori di minoranza: Federico Fornaro (Pd), Filiberto Zaratti (Avs), Carmela Auriemma (M5s), oltre a Magi. Oggi, a partire dalle 12, è previsto un unico voto sulle cinque pregiudiziali di costituzionalità chieste dalle opposizioni. A quanto si apprende, gli emendamenti presentati dalle opposizioni sono circa sessanta, gli stessi depositati in commissione agli articoli del testo modificati in Senato, anche se - con l'apposizione della fiducia - le proposte di modifica decadranno. Comunque, quello di oggi è un primo 'test' d'Aula per la tenuta della maggioranza, dato che probabilmente le minoranze chiederanno lo scrutinio segreto, come era stato a luglio sull'emendamento sulle preferenze, che poi è stato bocciato grazie a i 'franchi tiratori' tra le fila del centrodestra. Sul punto un esponente di centrodestra che segue il dossier dice di "non avere dubbi" sulla compattezza della maggioranza, anche in vista dei voti successivi nell'Aula di Montecitorio. E FdI serra i ranghi. "Mi sembra che Giorgia Meloni sia stata chiara. Se il provvedimento non passa si va a casa. La fiducia è stata messa per questo motivo", dice il capogruppo dei meloniani alla Camera, Galeazzo Bignami. In caso di bocciatura delle pregiudiziali dovrebbe riunirsi già oggi una Conferenza dei capigruppo, per fissare il timing dei lavori. Su tre dei quattro articoli modificati a Palazzo Madama, il governo dovrebbe porre la fiducia , che dovrebbe essere votata venerdì, con il voto palese. Mentre, un'altra 'prova' con lo scrutinio segreto è probabile con il voto finale sul provvedimento, che dovrebbe tenersi la prossima settimana, tra mercoledì e giovedì.

articles.body:
Closure of bridges struck by drones in Ukrainian capital causes traffic chaos.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called on allies to tighten sanctions against Russia after a wave of strikes triggered gridlock across Kyiv.

Traffic chaos gripped the Ukrainian capital on Friday after Russian drone attacks overnight closed key bridges. Zelenskyy called for allies to act to prevent Moscow from sourcing components for its arsenal as Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine face attacks around the clock.

- list 4 of 4UK arrests British-Iranian suspect over RAF ‘plot’: What we know

Kyiv’s Southern Bridge and Paton Bridge, key routes for cars and public transport across the Dnipro River, were closed in both directions after the attacks. The Metro Bridge was closed in the direction of Kyiv’s right bank, the city administration said.

Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that Iranian-type Shahed kamikaze drones struck the Southern Bridge “several times”. One person was killed as Russia launched more than 100 drones across the country.

The president, who has persistently called for additional help to boost Ukraine’s air defences during Moscow’s concentrated air campaign, noted that supply chains for such weapons trail through Europe, the United States, China and Japan.

“No matter how hard Moscow tries to fully localise the production of its drones and missiles, its ability to escalate remains critically dependent on foreign components,” Zelenskyy wrote. “Most of these companies are well-known manufacturers, but their components still make their way to Russia.”

“Every Russian drone can actually be stopped right at the production line. What is needed is the political will of these countries,” he continued. “If the Kremlin has chosen more strikes, sanctions must work and must be strengthened.”

Last month, European Union foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc was “working on new proposals to tighten sanctions enforcement” and implement new measures.

US President Donald Trump separately signed a sweeping Russian sanctions package into law, taking aim at Russian President Vladimir Putin, banks, other financial institutions, and the energy and defence sectors.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, Russian strikes targeted a kindergarten in Kherson, a grocery store in Kharkiv and apartment buildings in Kramatorsk and Sumy, Zelenskyy said.

The Dnipro, Odesa, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Poltava and Rivne regions also came under attack with at least four people reported wounded.

The Russian Ministry of Defence earlier said on Telegram that its drones hit a bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv, a power station in the surrounding region, the Izmail port near Odesa and a cargo vessel. It claimed all the sites were used for Ukrainian military purposes.

Ukraine’s military carried out its own overnight attacks on Russia and said they hit a Lukoil facility in the city of Volgograd as well as an oil dispatch station in the Samara region with fires breaking out at both sites.

Ukrainian forces also carried out missions in several other Russian regions that targeted airfields, industrial sites and other facilities, including in the Black Sea, Zelenskyy said.

Russian authorities in the Black Sea port town of Tuapse said an enterprise was damaged by drone debris, but they did not provide details.

articles.title: Who is the 'hero' Indian pilot who was stabbed on Israel-bound flight?
articles.summary: Capt Smit Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard the Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv.
articles.preview: The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar. Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia. The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia.
articles.body:
The pilot who was stabbed on an Israel-bound flight on Wednesday has been identified as Indian national Capt Smit Machchhar.

Machchhar was attacked by another pilot onboard a Flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, forcing the plane to divert to Saudi Arabia.

The captain, who has been hailed as a "true hero" by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, was taken to a hospital in Tabuk, a city in north-western Saudi Arabia.

Describing the events, Machchhar said he was on the floor and still being attacked when he realised the plane carrying more than 170 passengers was in a dive and he had to do something.

"I was lying on the floor injured but I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside," he told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi during a video call on Friday.

Years of experience

Machchhar grew up in the Indian city of Mumbai, where his parents still live. In 2008, he joined Mainland Air, an aviation college in New Zealand's Dunedin, before joining Indian airline SpiceJet as a commercial pilot three years later.

He moved to Dubai and joined Flydubai in 2022 as an experienced pilot.

Philip Kean, the CEO of Mainland Air, told the BBC he remembered Machchhar as a man who would remain calm in a crisis.

"We trained him for forced landing - not this kind of situation, which is very, very rare," Kean said. "It was a long time back but he came across as a good and honest worker."

Machchhar has more than 9,750 hours of flying experience, including more than 6,400 hours as pilot-in-command, according to his LinkedIn profile.

His former employer SpiceJet issued a statement calling Machchhar a "hero" who had saved "countless lives".

An old friend who worked with him at SpiceJet, Capt Dharav Gosalia, described him as outgoing and "very jovial".

Machchhar - whose nickname was "Smit Mac" - was a "disciplined flier" who had undergone years of training, he said, including from former Indian Air Force pilots who had moved into commercial aviation.

Last year, Machchhar spoke about how he started flying and his experiences as a pilot on a podcast called Bona-Fide Banter.

Aviation, he said, was "never a childhood dream". When he was around 19, he joined a management course, planning to work for his family's business. But then he came across an aviation seminar and "the bug bit [him]", he added.

Machchhar also spoke about how, when he wore his pilot's uniform, he was "no-nonsense" and thought "about work 100%". But unlike his younger days, he added, he now placed a greater value on having a healthy work-life balance and spending time with family.

"Give personal life equal importance - it will help you fly longer," he advised.

He also detailed challenges he had faced in the air, including when a passenger went into early labour and the crew worked together to ensure the baby was born safely.

"In aviation terms, I was lucky to grow up with people who helped me be the pilot that I am today," he said, crediting senior pilots with teaching him how to face stressful situations.

At the time of the conversation, Machchhar said that no plane he'd flown had needed to make an emergency landing. He had, however, faced medical emergencies and minor aircraft issues that had caused delays.

He said delays were "not my problem. As long as you're walking out of the aircraft [safely], that's what I want."

Indian social media has been awash with praise for Machchhar since his identity emerged, with commenters calling him a hero. Snippets from the podcast have also gone viral.

Stabbed mid-flight

Flydubai's flight FZ1073 took off from Dubai International Airport in the United Arab Emirates at 03:05 GMT (07:05 local time) en route to Ben Gurion Airport in Israel.

The flight was carrying at least 150 people, with Netanyahu saying "almost all" passengers were Israeli.

The Israeli prime minister later wrote on X that Machchhar had "saved the lives of 174 people" and prevented "a catastrophic mid-air disaster".

Data from flight tracking website Flightradar24 shows the plane made a rapid descent over Saudi Arabia around two and a half hours after take-off, dropping more than 17,000ft (5,000m) in less than two minutes at around 05:21.

Minutes later, the plane signalled an emergency code - squawk 7700 - before switching it to a squawk 7500 code, which indicates a hijacking.

At 05:40, the plane - which had briefly entered Jordanian airspace - looped back into Saudi Arabia, where it later started its manual descent for landing.

Less than an hour later, the plane returned to squawk 7700.

Initial local media reports cited Israeli officials as saying a fight had broken out between two pilots.

But speaking on Wednesday after the incident, Netanyahu confirmed later reports that one pilot had stabbed the other before "apparently trying to crash" the plane.

He said an Israeli passenger told him "the plane went into a spin and began to descend" before the passenger and a crew member broke into the cockpit and overpowered the "pilot who had carried out the stabbing".

The plane was diverted to Tabuk Airport in north-western Saudi Arabia and touched down at 06:58, according to location data.

The stabbed pilot, who has since been airlifted to Abu Dhabi, was later identified as Machchhar. The Indian embassy in the United Arab Emirates said he was "in good health and recovering well".

In his call with Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Machchhar said he had been flying planes for 17 years and "can tell what is happening to the plane even with my eyes closed".

Speaking about his recovery, the pilot said he is "looking at it as a journey" - saying that it "will take time" but he is "confident that the recovery will be there and I will become fit and healthy again".

Modi and Trump praise Machchhar

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said Machchhar "showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others" despite being seriously injured.

"His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy," he wrote in a post on X, adding that he hoped for the pilot's speedy recovery.

And during their call, Modi told Machchhar that "his courage, patience and quick decision-making saved the lives of so many people" and the whole country was proud of him.

Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar praised the pilot's "extraordinary courage and remarkable presence of mind, even in the face of grave danger".

Ambassador Deepak Mittal said he was "proud of Capt Smit for his bravery" and "very reassured" to meet him.

US President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House that "the pilot was in very bad shape" but had the sense to open the cockpit door during the attack.

"Amazing, in a way he was a hero, to open the door. He was able to fall back and get the door open."

articles.title: Traffico in tilt a Kiev dopo gli attacchi russi ai ponti. Zelensky: 'Usa e Ue non fanno abbastanza'
articles.summary: Il presidente ucraino: 'Putin ha dato ordine di non seguire più le regole di guerra'
articles.preview: Un edificio residenziale di 25 piani nel quartiere di Darnytskyi a Kiev è stato danneggiato a seguito di un attacco russo. Una persona è morta. "Un edificio residenziale di 25 piani è stato danneggiato nel quartiere di Darnytskyi a seguito di un attacco nemico. Sono in corso accertamenti sull'identità delle vittime", si legge nel rapporto. Successivamente, il Kmwa ha aggiunto: "Purtroppo, una persona è morta a seguito di un attacco nemico contro un edificio residenziale nel distretto di Darnytskyi".
articles.body:
Un edificio residenziale di 25 piani nel quartiere di Darnytskyi a Kiev è stato danneggiato a seguito di un attacco russo. Una persona è morta. "Un edificio residenziale di 25 piani è stato danneggiato nel quartiere di Darnytskyi a seguito di un attacco nemico. Sono in corso accertamenti sull'identità delle vittime", si legge nel rapporto. Successivamente, il Kmwa ha aggiunto: "Purtroppo, una persona è morta a seguito di un attacco nemico contro un edificio residenziale nel distretto di Darnytskyi".

Nelle prime ore del mattino un attacco russo contro Kiev ha colpito nuovamente il Ponte Sud della capitale ucraina, già bersagliato più volte nella giornata di ieri. Finestre di un edificio non residenziale e diverse automobili sono state danneggiate. A Kiev dunque il traffico dei mezzi pubblici è temporaneamente limitato su alcuni ponti, ha fatto sapere l'amministrazione cittadina tramite Telegram. Il Ponte Sud, in particolare, è chiuso in entrambe le direzioni; il ponte della metropolitana è chiuso in direzione della riva destra. Il Comune ha comunicato ai cittadini le modifiche al trasporto pubblico.

Il traffico a Kiev è andato in tilt dopo la chiusura di uno dei ponti principali della città e l'imposizione di restrizioni su altri, in seguito a una nuova ondata di attacchi russi con droni. I reporter dell'Afp hanno osservato lunghe code di auto e autobus bloccati sulle arterie principali della capitale ucraina, mentre i pendolari cercavano percorsi alternativi.

Il congestionamento è stato causato dalla chiusura totale al traffico, in entrambe le direzioni, del Ponte Sud (Pivdennyi Mist), uno degli otto ponti che collegano la parte orientale e quella occidentale di Kiev attraversando il fiume Dnipro. Il Ponte Paton, situato più a nord, è rimasto aperto in un solo senso di marcia, ha dichiarato il sindaco Vitali Klitschko, senza tuttavia segnalare danni alla struttura.

Ieri i droni russi hanno colpito le strutture portanti del Ponte Sud. Il passaggio è stato chiuso temporaneamente per consentire una valutazione strutturale. Sebbene avesse riaperto al traffico veicolare e alla metropolitana poco dopo, il ponte ha subito nuovi attacchi con droni nella notte appena trascorsa, ha riferito Klitschko. Il secondo attacco notturno ha danneggiato un pilone, il manto stradale e una barriera protettiva in calcestruzzo lungo la linea della metropolitana, ha aggiunto il sindaco. Dall'inizio dell'invasione russa su vasta scala nel febbraio 2022, l'Ucraina teme da tempo attacchi ai suoi principali ponti di collegamento.

Zelensky, 'Putin ha dato ordine di non seguire più le regole di guerra'

Secondo informazioni intercettate da Kiev, Vladimir Putin ha ordinato ai suoi comandanti militari di abbandonare le regole di guerra, provocando un forte aumento degli attacchi contro obiettivi civili nel contesto di una grande offensiva volta a riconquistare il vantaggio nel conflitto. Lo ha detto il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky parlando con il Financial Times. "Ha detto che ora non ci sono più regole", ha affermato Zelensky, riferendosi alle informazioni di intelligence che includevano intercettazioni di comunicazioni di funzionari del Cremlino. L'intervista è avvenuta nella scuola di Kiev colpita ieri da un attacco russo. Zelensky ha affermato che Putin ha dato l'ordine a settembre, quando la Russia ha iniziato a intensificare i suoi attacchi aerei su Kiev, colpendo scuole, ospedali e centri dati.

Zelensky al Ft, 'i nostri partner non fanno abbastanza per l'Ucraina'

I partner dell'Ucraina stanno facendo "non abbastanza, ovviamente non abbastanza" per aiutare Kiev: lo ha detto al Financial Times il presidente Volodymyr Zelensky. Zelensky ha criticato i governi statunitense ed europeo, scrive il quotidiano economico, per quella che ha definito una volontà politica insufficiente nel costringere Putin a porre fine alla guerra, sostenendo che i partner dell'Ucraina possedevano la leva economica e diplomatica necessaria per esercitare una maggiore pressione su Mosca.

articles.title: Washington’s diplomacy in Sudan has backfired
articles.summary: Pressure meant to isolate Sudan’s army has instead left Washington isolated and a ceasefire further out of reach.
articles.preview: Pressure meant to isolate Sudan’s army has instead left Washington isolated and a ceasefire further out of reach. After more than three years, Washington continues to fumble its way through a response to Sudan’s heart-wrenching war. This past week, it may have inadvertently backed itself into a diplomatic corner that offers no options for either itself or Sudan’s army to exit, putting a ceasefire even further out of reach.
articles.body:
Pressure meant to isolate Sudan’s army has instead left Washington isolated and a ceasefire further out of reach.

After more than three years, Washington continues to fumble its way through a response to Sudan’s heart-wrenching war. This past week, it may have inadvertently backed itself into a diplomatic corner that offers no options for either itself or Sudan’s army to exit, putting a ceasefire even further out of reach.

As world leaders gathered in New York for the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly, Washington pressed hard on the leaders of the Sudanese armed forces (SAF) to sign an unconditional ceasefire that would freeze the conflict and allow unimpeded access for critical aid deliveries.

In the past, the rebel Rapid Support Forces militia, using the ample diplomatic and public relations support from its chief regional backer, has been quick to agree to any deal that puts it on equal footing with the national army it is seeking to unseat. But with no intention or ability to implement the terms of any ceasefire, the RSF’s commitment to peace is likely worth what one would expect from a mercenary army that has committed multiple rounds of genocide. Still, United States officials repeatedly refer to the RSF in diplomatic circles as the more “cooperative party”.

In that light, since earlier this year, Washington’s pressure campaign has been focused on the SAF almost exclusively in the misguided belief that sufficient pressure would bring the army to its knees and cause it to abandon its effort to liberate the millions of Sudan’s civilians trapped under RSF rule. But 20 years of comprehensive US sanctions on Sudan, far more biting and wide-ranging than anything Presidents Donald Trump’s or Joe Biden’s administrations have imposed, should have taught the Trump team that sanctions in Sudan are not instruments to be used tactically. This is a regime capable of withstanding US pressure over the long run.

Nonetheless, a new round of US sanctions against SAF military procurement networks in June was followed by the imposition of chemical weapons sanctions in July despite the lack of any credible attempt to investigate the facts of their use on the ground. Later, in August, the US added to its punitive approach by tabling a new initiative at the UN to impose a countrywide arms embargo, updating the Darfur arms embargo dating from the first Darfur genocide in the early 2000s, which the RSF and its regional backers have flouted on a nearly daily basis since the start of the war.

Washington’s latest move was widely interpreted as an unbalanced attempt to target the army’s supply networks that had recently enabled a number of critical battlefield victories for the SAF and created a shift in momentum in the conflict. But lacking the minimum votes from even half the UN Security Council to expand the embargo in addition to the likely prospect of a Russian veto, the US agreed to a one-month technical extension of the current embargo in the hope that an additional month of lobbying would add supporters to its initiative. It won’t.

The final piece of Washington’s maximum pressure campaign came last week when it chose to tighten its noose around Khartoum by making General Abdel Fattah al-Burhan’s attendance at the General Assembly contingent upon his signing of Washington’s stale ceasefire deal. Acts of diplomatic blackmail are high-risk gambits and, in this case, reflect more Washington’s own deep embarrassment and growing frustration at failing to get a deal signed than the army’s intransigence.

Since Washington first tabled its ceasefire proposal in the days leading up to last year’s UN General Assembly, it has been repeatedly stymied by both sides’ unwillingness to sign. But fighters are going to fight. Especially if they believe that the deal they are meant to sign only allows the other side to regroup and rearm. Indeed, a ceasefire signed in a vacuum that offers neither side a glimpse of their respective futures is more likely to entrench the de facto partition that already divides the country.

That is clearly an outcome that benefits the Rapid Support Forces, which is eager to formalise its rule over large swaths of the country, more than Sudan’s army, which argues that it is fighting to make the country whole again.

The often-repeated belief held by Washington that both sides are continuing to fight because they think they can achieve a total military victory misdiagnoses each side’s motivations. They fight because they believe they have to win to ensure their own survival.

This motivation to fight was only given further fuel by the US Department of State’s hastily issued statement in the midst of the UN’s marathon meetings last week, arguing that, “Neither the Sudanese Armed Forces, the Rapid Support Forces, nor their respective leaders, represent legitimate, constitutional governance for Sudan – they rule through force of arms alone. The conduct of each leader of the warring factions renders them ineligible to govern the country.”

This may be true in the long term, but it is hardly a diplomatically smart tactic to employ if trying to persuade either side to lay down their arms in the near term. Instead, the statement appears intended more as an ex post facto justification for Washington’s latest diplomatic sleight of hand in barring al-Burhan from delivering his country’s address to the UN General Assembly.

Leave aside the breach of international law and diplomatic protocol or the policy inconsistency that saw leaders from military juntas across Africa, not to mention an Iranian delegation, receive visas to New York. Washington’s choice appears to be more than a simple strong-arm tactic to achieve a ceasefire and raises the question of whether it is ratcheting up its pressure even further to the only place left for it to go by trying to bring about more immediate regime change in the country.

Taken alongside the manifold measures this year to punish, isolate and delegitimise Sudan’s army, the argument is hard to ignore. But here too, a US approach that has largely been driven by tactics and not strategy risks making solutions even more difficult to achieve. Already, Washington’s move has left it isolated among the broad Western, Arab and African coalitions that are pressing not merely for a quick ceasefire but for a more comprehensive and lasting peace that will return Sudan to a stable national and regional footing.

Many countries have since expressed quiet disappointment that the US missed an important opportunity for diplomacy, not for al-Burhan to express his views on the war but for the military leader to hear loudly and collectively the calls for peace from dozens of assembled world leaders. Most serious was Saudi Arabia’s warning that it would review its participation in the US-led Quad initiative going forward.

The Trump administration has little progress to show since it announced last summer its ambition to bring peace to Sudan. Instead, the administration appears to be making many of the same mistakes past US peacemaking efforts have made by believing that diplomatic pressure alone will shape battlefield outcomes and aid the cause of peace.

Last week, Washington took this approach to an extreme. But the isolation intended for Sudan’s army has ricocheted back onto Washington. Reversing course and engaging the war’s belligerents are today not merely necessary for the US to save face and maintain a diplomatic coalition it aims to lead, but they are the only thing that will save lives in Sudan.

articles.title: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties as northern conflict escalates
articles.summary: The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian forces battle rebel fighters across its northern region.
articles.preview: Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict. On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security. Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.
articles.body:
Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict.

On Thursday, Ethiopia announced that it was closing its embassy in the Eritrean capital, Asmara, and ordered 10 Eritrean diplomats to leave the country within 48 hours, accusing them of activities that threatened national security.

Eritrea responded by cutting diplomatic relations, saying Ethiopia's decision had left it with no choice but to take reciprocal action.

The diplomatic confrontation came hours after powerful explosions were heard overnight in Ethiopian capital, Addis Ababa, including near Ethiopia's military headquarters.

It follows a sharp deterioration in relations between the neighbours, with Ethiopia accusing Eritrea of supporting a new rebel alliance â an allegation Asmara has repeatedly denied.

Eritrea described the decision to expel its ambassador as "astounding".

"Eritrea has no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia," its foreign ministry said, warning of "negative corollaries" from the decision.

The diplomatic fallout comes as Ethiopian federal forces battle fighters from the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies across parts of the northern regions of Tigray, Afar and Amhara.

Ethiopia has also expelled an Egyptian diplomat, giving him 48 hours to leave the country, according to state media. The government has not publicly given a reason for the decision.

Egypt responded by ordering an Ethiopian embassy official to leave within the same period, according to the state-affiliated Al Qahera News.

Relations between Ethiopia and Egypt have been strained for years, largely over Ethiopia's Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD), a huge hydroelectric project on the Blue Nile.

Egypt, which relies heavily on the Nile for its water supplies, has long expressed concern about the dam's potential impact on its share of the river's water.

- How fresh fighting in Tigray could spark wider conflict in Ethiopia

- Published2 hours ago

- WATCH: Why are Ethiopia's rebels joining forces?

- Published4 days ago

The cutting of ties between Ethiopia and Eritrea mark a dramatic reversal from 2018, when Abiy restored relations with Asmara after two decades of hostility, prompting joyous scenes as the border reopened and families separated for years were reunited.

The rapprochement helped earn the Ethiopian prime minister the Nobel Peace Prize in 2019.

The latest hostilities are the most serious since a peace agreement ended the devastating Tigray war in 2022. An African Union mediator previously estimated that about 600,000 people had died during that two-year conflict.

Last month, the TPLF joined six other armed movements, including the Fano militia from Amhara, to form an alliance whose stated objective is to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government from power.

A pro-government militia commander fighting in Tigray told the BBC that Eritrean soldiers had been involved on the front lines.

The BBC has not independently verified the allegation.

The BBC is unable to report from Tigray and the internet has been cut, making it difficult to get reliable information from the region. It is not clear who was responsible for cutting communications.

In a rare response to the BBC before diplomatic relations were severed, Eritrea's Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied that it was involved in the fighting in Tigray, which borders his country.

He told BBC Tigrinya that Ethiopia's governing Prosperity Party was blaming neighbouring countries to divert attention from conflicts and other problems within Ethiopia.

The two countries were allies during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces against the TPLF.

But relations have deteriorated significantly since then, particularly over Ethiopia's push for direct access to the Red Sea.

Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993.

Abiy has repeatedly argued that access to the sea is essential to Ethiopia's long-term economic and security interests, while Eritrea has accused his government of harbouring ambitions over its ports.

Federal forces and their allies appear to have made gains in southern Tigray and are advancing towards Mekelle, the regional capital. In Alamata, a doctor told the BBC earlier this week that at least 52 civilians had been killed during three days of intense fighting.

The TPLF has also been fighting in neighbouring Afar, which lies along Ethiopia's crucial transport corridor to Djibouti and the sea. Tens of thousands of people are estimated to have fled their homes there.

Both the Ethiopian government and the TPLF accuse the other of starting the latest hostilities. Tigrayan authorities say their forces were responding to a federal offensive and drone strikes, while Addis Ababa says Tigrayan fighters launched attacks after taking control of federally administered airports in Tigray.

The African Union has urged Ethiopia, Eritrea and Egypt to exercise restraint and resolve their differences through diplomatic channels, warning against actions that could further destabilise the region.

The UN has also warned that the deteriorating security situation is severely disrupting humanitarian work in northern Ethiopia. UN spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said drone activity and air strikes were putting civilians, vital infrastructure and aid operations at risk, while insecurity and road closures were restricting humanitarian movements.

The UN has called on all sides to guarantee safe and unhindered access to people in need.

articles.title: Il racconto del pilota-eroe del Flydubai: 'Ho aperto la porta della cabina mentre ero sotto attacco'
articles.summary: L'indiano Machchhar: 'Se non avessi mostrato coraggio, 170 persone sarebbero morte'
articles.preview: Il pilota indiano Smit Machchhar ha dichiarato, in una videochiamata con il premier indiano Narendra Modi, di aver aperto la porta della cabina di pilotaggio dell'aereo Flydubai mentre era a terra e di essere ancora sotto attacco da parte del suo copilota. "Avevo riportato numerose ferite - racconta l'uomo, come riporta il quotidiano israeliano Ynet - ma mi sono detto che dovevo alzarmi e agire. Quando sono caduto, ho sentito l'aereo precipitare. In quel momento ho trovato la forza di aprire la porta della cabina. Stavo lottando per la mia vita.
articles.body:
Il pilota indiano Smit Machchhar ha dichiarato, in una videochiamata con il premier indiano Narendra Modi, di aver aperto la porta della cabina di pilotaggio dell'aereo Flydubai mentre era a terra e di essere ancora sotto attacco da parte del suo copilota. "Avevo riportato numerose ferite - racconta l'uomo, come riporta il quotidiano israeliano Ynet - ma mi sono detto che dovevo alzarmi e agire. Quando sono caduto, ho sentito l'aereo precipitare. In quel momento ho trovato la forza di aprire la porta della cabina. Stavo lottando per la mia vita. Mi sono reso conto che se non avessi mostrato coraggio, 170 passeggeri sarebbero morti".

Il capitano parla dal letto di ospedale con la testa fasciata, i tubicini ancora al naso. "Altri sono intervenuti - ha affermato parlando in tv con Modi in dichiarazioni riprese dalla Bbc - e hanno svolto un ruolo (nel controllo della situazione, ndr). Io, ovviamente, lottavo per la mia vita, ma allo stesso tempo sapevo che non avrei permesso che altri morissero".

Modi ha detto al capitano che "il suo coraggio, la sua pazienza e la sua prontezza nel prendere decisioni hanno salvato la vita a moltissime persone" e che l'intero Paese è orgoglioso di lui.

Il capitano è stato inizialmente trasportato in un ospedale di Tabuk in Arabia Saudita e poi trasportato in aereo ad Abu Dhabi, dove le sue condizioni sono stabili.

articles.title: Seoul warns 'further action' if Ukraine does not apologise over prisoner-of-war row
articles.summary: President Lee Jae Myung also accused Kyiv of "attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula".
articles.preview: South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South. Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret. Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.
articles.body:
South Korea's President Lee Jae Myung has threatened to take unspecified "further action" if Ukraine does not issue a public apology for revealing that two North Korean prisoners of war had been sent to the South.

Ukraine's leader Volodymyr Zelensky made the disclosure to the UN general assembly last week, angering Seoul, who said the move was meant to stay secret.

Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Thursday described the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding", adding that Kyiv was "working" to resolve it.

Lee rejected this characterisation on X, saying it concerned "the dignity of the Korean people and the nation".

Lee's office said last week that it was Ukraine that requested for the move to be kept secret, partly to protect the North Koreans' families, and also because Kyiv wanted to avoid criticism that it had given up an opportunity to exchange the soldiers for Ukrainian prisoners of war.

Zelensky's office responded, saying the two countries had no such agreement to keep the move confidential, further escalating the situation.

Lee himself faced heavy criticism at home after Zelensky's disclosure, with the South Korean opposition accusing him of covering up the transfer to appease Pyongyang.

The two soldiers, who were among thousands of North Koreans supporting Russia in the Ukraine war, had earlier told local media they wanted to be sent to South Korea.

Speaking to Ukrainian media on Thursday, Sybiha, the foreign minister, said he "hopes that this situation will be resolved in the very near future".

"We are working on it. For us, South Korea is an important country. And I really hope for momentum, continuation, and concrete results that we are truly achieving with them," he said.

Lee, in response, accused Kyiv of attempting to "bring war on the Korean Peninsula".

"We express serious regret that, instead of acknowledging the facts of the agreement and apologising, they are talking about an imminent military clash between the North and South," he said in an X post.

Seoul has been sympathetic to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion, but has adhered to its longstanding policy of not providing lethal weapons to any country engaged in active war.

articles.title: Allontanarsi dal precipizio
articles.summary: I rischi di una nuova guerra sono molto alti perché rispetto al passato la regione è più instabile, avverte un settimanale etiope
articles.preview: L’Etiopia settentrionale si trova di nuovo sull’orlo di una catastrofe. Gli ultimi scontri tra le forze armate del governo etiope e il Fronte popolare di liberazione del Tigrai indicano che la tregua precaria raggiunta quattro anni fa si sta sgretolando e che i compromessi hanno lasciato il posto a una mentalità a “somma zero”. Con l’intensificarsi dei movimenti militari, entrambe le parti si sono lanciate in recriminazioni, accusandosi a vicenda di aver sparato il primo colpo.
articles.body:
L’Etiopia settentrionale si trova di nuovo sull’orlo di una catastrofe. Gli ultimi scontri tra le forze armate del governo etiope e il Fronte popolare di liberazione del Tigrai indicano che la tregua precaria raggiunta quattro anni fa si sta sgretolando e che i compromessi hanno lasciato il posto a una mentalità a “somma zero”. Con l’intensificarsi dei movimenti militari, entrambe le parti si sono lanciate in recriminazioni, accusandosi a vicenda di aver sparato il primo colpo. Tuttavia soffermarsi su chi abbia premuto per primo il grilletto è una pericolosa distrazione. Quello che conta ora è la terrificante realtà verso cui porterà questo conflitto se non sarà fermato subito: il completo collasso istituzionale e sofferenze inimmaginabili.

Non ci sono dubbi: la ripresa degli scontri segna la fine dell’accordo di pace firmato a Pretoria, in Sudafrica, nel 2022. Il patto era di far tacere le armi, facilitare il ritorno dell’ordine costituzionale, disarmare i combattenti e garantire l’arrivo di aiuti umanitari. Invece gli impegni politici non sono stati rispettati, si è diffuso un clima di sfiducia e una fragile pace si è disintegrata.

Le ripercussioni si fanno già sentire. La sospensione dei voli commerciali della Ethiopian Airlines verso i principali aeroporti del Tigrai e l’interruzione dei servizi di telecomunicazione mostrano una spirale oscura e fin troppo familiare, perché significa isolare dal mondo esterno una popolazione già vulnerabile, tagliando le linee dei rifornimenti e le arterie commerciali. Se non sarà fermata, questa nuova guerra potrebbe avere conseguenze umanitarie, politiche, economiche e diplomatiche ancora più gravi di quella del 2020–2022. Durante il precedente conflitto si stima che siano morte 600mila persone, con milioni di sfollati e il tessuto della nazione lacerato. In un contesto già reso difficile dall’inflazione, dagli sfollamenti interni e da una siccità persistente potrebbe scoppiare un caos economico. Dal punto di vista politico, un’altra guerra su vasta scala rischia di mandare in pezzi il contratto sociale, creando dei vuoti di potere che nessuna vittoria militare potrà mai colmare.

Influenze esterne

A rendere particolarmente pericolosa la situazione è la rete di intrecci regionali. Rispetto alla guerra precedente, gli allineamenti politici e geopolitici nel Corno d’Africa sono cambiati. La vicina Eritrea, dove i leader nutrono animosità verso Addis Abeba e fanno calcoli strategici riguardo al nord dell’Etiopia, resta una catalizzatrice d’instabilità. Allo stesso tempo la guerra civile in Sudan ha trasformato quello tra i due paesi in un confine poroso, attraversato da un flusso incontrollato di armi e insorti. Che si tratti di stati confinanti o di gruppi armati locali, il coinvolgimento o l’uso di combattenti per procura esterni minaccia di trasformare una disputa interna in una conflagrazione regionale incontrollabile. La risposta della comunità internazionale deve essere rapida, chiara e decisa. La via della guerra è già stata percorsa e porta solo alla rovina. La via del dialogo è indubbiamente piena di difficoltà e compromessi, e richiede ai leader di mettere da parte orgoglio e ambizioni politiche. Le parti in conflitto devono fare un passo indietro dal baratro. Ai libri di storia non interesserà chi ha sparato per primo, ma solo se i leader di questa generazione avranno avuto il coraggio di fermare gli scontri prima che non ci fosse più nulla da salvare. ◆

Il 29 settembre il presidente di Futuro Nazionale Roberto Vannacci è stato ospite di Porta a Porta, su Rai1, dove ha commentato i risultati delle elezioni suppletive a Reggio Calabria e le principali questioni del dibattito politico. Tra le altre cose, Vannacci è tornato ad affrontare il tema della guerra in Ucraina, ribadendo la necessità di interrompere il sostegno militare al governo di Volodymir Zelensky.

A sostegno della sua posizione, Vannacci ha ricostruito (-1:29:40) quelle che sarebbero le cause del nuovo conflitto in Ucraina, iniziato dopo l’invasione russa partita il 24 febbraio 2022. «I problemi tra l’Ucraina e la Russia sono cominciati nel 2008 in seguito al vertice della NATO che ha invitato l’Ucraina ad aderire alla NATO», ha detto Vannacci. Secondo il leader di Futuro Nazionale, in quel vertice ci sarebbe stato «l’avvio delle trattative» per l’adesione non solo dell’Ucraina, ma della Georgia e della Moldavia, cosa che non sarebbe stata gradita dal presidente russo Vladimir Putin, che temeva l’allargamento a Est dell’Organizzazione del Trattato dell’Atlantico del Nord (ossia la NATO, ndr). Vannacci ha poi aggiunto che la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato tre «ultimatum» dati da Putin prima dell’invasione. «L’Ucraina non entra nella NATO, non vengono schierate truppe della NATO in Ucraina, non vengono schierati sistemi a lunga gittata della NATO in Ucraina», queste sono le condizioni che Putin avrebbe dato secondo Vannacci e che però non sarebbero state accettate.

Ma le cose stanno davvero così? In breve: Vannacci semplifica troppo le cause del conflitto in Ucraina, creando una narrazione non supportata nel complesso dalle fonti ufficiali. L’affermazione secondo cui i problemi tra Russia e Ucraina sarebbero cominciati nel 2008, in seguito alla decisione della NATO di aprire all’ingresso dell’Ucraina, contiene una parte di verità ma la tesi secondo cui la NATO e l’Ucraina non avrebbero accettato gli “ultimatum” di Putin è fuorviante.

articles.title: Non sono stati sequestrati 140 milioni di dollari negli uffici dell’ex responsabile degli appalti per la difesa ucraina
articles.summary: È una notizia falsa diffusa da un falso sito di un media ucraino e rilanciata dalla propaganda russa
articles.preview: Il 25 settembre 2026 su Facebook è stato pubblicato un presunto servizio del media ucraino The New Voice of Ukraine (NV) in cui una voce di donna fuori campo racconta che l’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina (NABU) avrebbe trovato e «sequestrato oltre 140 milioni di dollari in contanti, stipati in diversi cartoni per frigoriferi» durante un blitz negli uffici di Arsen Zhumadilov, ex capo dell’Agenzia per gli appalti della difesa dimessosi lo scorso 31 agosto in relazione ad accuse di sprechi, frodi e corruzione.
articles.body:
Il 25 settembre 2026 su Facebook è stato pubblicato un presunto servizio del media ucraino The New Voice of Ukraine (NV) in cui una voce di donna fuori campo racconta che l’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina (NABU) avrebbe trovato e «sequestrato oltre 140 milioni di dollari in contanti, stipati in diversi cartoni per frigoriferi» durante un blitz negli uffici di Arsen Zhumadilov, ex capo dell’Agenzia per gli appalti della difesa dimessosi lo scorso 31 agosto in relazione ad accuse di sprechi, frodi e corruzione.

Il servizio continua aggiungendo che su una di queste scatole era stata apposta «un’etichetta con la scritta “Servitore del Popolo”», cioè il nome della serie televisiva satirica scritta e interpretata nel 2015 da Volodymyr Zelensky prima di entrare in politica ed essere eletto nel 2019 presidente dell’Ucraina.

Nel filmato si vedono anche presunti agenti della NABU entrare in una stanza dove si trovano diversi grandi scatoloni con mazzette da 10mila dollari ciascuna. Attaccato all’esterno di uno di essi, si vede un biglietto in ucraino con la scritta «Servitore del Popolo».

È una notizia falsa.

Non esiste alcun riscontro su media credibili e affidabili di un’operazione del NABU negli uffici di Zhumadilov in cui sarebbero stati trovati scatoloni con dentro 140 milioni di dollari. Inoltre, il filmato che mostra gli agenti NABU con gli scatoloni pieni di dollari contiene incongruenze ed errori tipici dei prodotti IA: ad esempio, le mani degli agenti risultano sfocate e non definite in maniera realistica e in ogni mazzetta compare una fascetta con scritte in inglese che contengono in alcuni casi non lettere ma segni incomprensibili.

L’Ufficio nazionale anticorruzione dell’Ucraina ha smentito il 25 settembre 2026 ufficialmente la veridicità di questa notizia infondata, aggiungendo che la scena presente nel video virale che mostra agenti del NABU ritrovare scatoloni pieni di soldi è stata generata con l’intelligenza artificiale. Anche The New Voice of Ukraine ha smentito lo stesso giorno di aver mai pubblicato una simile notizia.

Come hanno ricostruito i fact-checker spagnoli di Maldita e statunitensi di Lead Stories il video in questione attribuito a The New Voice of Ukraine è inizialmente comparso il 23 settembre in un falso sito (ora non più disponibile online, ma qui si può vedere una copia cache) per far credere di essere il media ucraino, creato il 21 settembre (cioè due giorni prima la diffusione della falsa notizia) e avente come dominio «nvukraine.com». Il dominio autentico di The New Voice of Ukraine è invece «nv.ua».

La falsa notizia è stata poi rilanciata il 24 settembre da canali russi su Telegram e ripresa su X in inglese il giorno successivo da una serie di account di propaganda e disinformazione filorussa.

articles.body:
San Antonio City Councilmember Ric Galvan remembers when data centers first arrived in his city in the 2000s, looking like relatively unassuming office buildings. But that’s changed in recent years, as data centers have grown into massive “hyperscale” facilities spanning millions of square feet and housing the physical infrastructure for AI.

Microsoft is expanding ‘biomimicry’ at its data centers as it faces more pushback from locals over construction, pollution, and noise.

There are now more than a dozen data centers in Galvan’s roughly 55-square-mile district, and he expects that number to grow to around 20 over the next few years if proposed projects are completed. They’re clustered along two main roads, concentrating nuisances in the same neighborhoods: traffic and trees cut down during construction, followed by constant bright lights and noise when the data center is operating.

A lot of the area used to be green fields, he explains, allowing many residents to feel close to nature. Now, he says, “that [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

“That [feeling] gets taken away pretty quickly when you make a gigantic data center.”

Across the US, more and more communities are rising up against these hulking data warehouses — protesting the effects they could have on quality of life, pollution, water, and electricity bills. Tech companies have responded with promises to mitigate any potential harm by paying for infrastructure upgrades needed in local water and power systems.

Microsoft is also taking a different approach to soften the impact its data centers have. It announced plans to make its data centers less jarring to local communities and the environment through what it describes as “biomimicry.”

Biomimicry is sort of a catch-all term for many of the ways technologies take inspiration from nature, from “painless” needles that imitate a mosquito’s proboscis to naturally ventilated buildings modeled after termite mounds. In Microsoft’s case, biomimicry involves “blending our datacenters into the natural landscape” to “create resilient ecosystems that support biodiversity, strengthen community ties, and help our datacenters become better neighbors.”

Essentially, Microsoft wants to make its data centers greener, literally, with more gardens and native trees on-site. It’s also promising to invest in projects that repair damaged ecosystems where it has data centers. The company thinks these efforts will limit problems its facilities have caused for neighbors, like noise pollution and the loss of green space.

It’s a nice gesture, advocates and sustainability experts tell me. Microsoft has tried to set itself apart from its rivals by engaging more with communities where it builds data centers. The strategy has appeased some local concerns — depending on whom you ask.

But these data centers are expanding so fast that they’ve simultaneously razed thousands of trees, and Microsoft’s greenhouse gas emissions are growing with the energy demands of AI. Advocates and residents near these data centers want to see more from the company to limit its larger impact on communities and the environment.

Zooming in

“Maybe … they’re trying to just make sure that they’re covering their bases,” Galvan says. “But also, I think if that’s the case, that’s fine,” he adds — as long as Microsoft and other data center operators are actually addressing concerns residents have brought up for years around pollution, water use, and the destruction of natural green spaces.

Microsoft has operated data centers in the Greater San Antonio area for almost a decade, and is spending hundreds of millions of dollars to build several more. In 2022, the company upset residents in San Antonio when it cut down more than 2,600 trees across a 33-acre expanse to build a data center. That — along with Microsoft’s requests for a zoning change and tax incentive — was a big controversy, Galvan says.

“We’re very proud of our trees here,” Galvan says, pointing out that the tree canopy also helps to mitigate heat, which in Texas is a growing problem. “So it was very frustrating to see that completely decimated.” (In an email, Microsoft spokesperson Jennifer Lyons that the company is “investing in enhancement projects that includes 400+ acres of woodland and pollinator prairie restoration” in San Antonio with a goal of leaving “land more productive than we received it.”)

Microsoft says it has more than 300 data centers in more than 34 countries and started biomimicry projects at a data center in the Netherlands in 2022. Now it plans to bring “nature-inspired solutions to restore and enhance natural ecosystems” to more than 20 sites in the US and Germany, and says it will do the same for all new projects in the US and “a growing number around the world.”

“We’re actually customizing the solutions to fit in with the local habitat and enhance what’s already there and restore what might have been lost in the past,” Kaitlin Chuzi, director of global land strategy at Microsoft, says.

In its September announcement, Microsoft references successes it has had in Mount Pleasant, Wisconsin, where the company is repurposing the shuttered Foxconn LCD factory property for its own data centers. In 2023, Microsoft funded a $4.2 million project to restore the flow of a creek that runs through its property, working with the Root-Pike Watershed Initiative Network (Root-Pike WIN) to do so — an example of the company working with locals to restore ecosystems.

Root-Pike WIN executive director Dave Giordano was also pleasantly surprised to see Microsoft outfit stormwater ponds on its property with forebays to prevent sediment from escaping. “That’s rare around here,” he says. “Not all data center companies are the same. Not all of them think like Microsoft.”

Councilmember Galvan also acknowledges that Microsoft has made itself more approachable by employing a local representative for the company who responds to community concerns. “That’s very different than other data centers in our city,” he says. In January, Microsoft introduced a five-point plan called “Community-First AI Infrastructure” meant to prevent its data centers from overwhelming a locale’s ability to cope with the company’s energy and water demands.

“Not all data center companies are the same.”

In San Antonio, Microsoft is also considering planting pollinator gardens to help monarch butterflies during their annual migrations. Another tactic Microsoft is considering at more sites as part of its biomimicry initiative is to create buffers of plants around its data centers to muffle some of the noise from humming servers and generators and to “minimize the visual impact on communities near our data centers,” says Chuzi.

In other words, it seems Microsoft aims to make its data centers less ugly and intrusive. But the mismatch between Microsoft’s smaller-scale nature-based proposals and the company’s broader impact on the environment and already limited resources leaves some advocates unsatisfied.

“I have nothing bad to say about nature-based solutions that are sensitive to the native ecosystem,” says Adrian Shelley, Texas director at consumer advocacy group Public Citizen. “All of that is good and is positive. However, I think that it’s, you know, basically lipstick on a pig.”

Shelley is particularly upset about pollution from new gas plants built to power data centers. In June, for example, Microsoft inked a 20-year agreement with Chevron to power a new AI data center campus in West Texas. The project is expected to be “among the largest co-located natural gas power and data center developments” in the nation, according to Chevron.

“I cannot really see any level of biomimicry investment that makes a gas plant a desirable neighbor,” Shelley says.

Proposed data centers are driving up electricity demand, spurring the development of new gas infrastructure. But Shelley is afraid Texans will be left to foot the bill for abandoned energy projects if the AI bubble bursts.

With Public Citizen’s backing, Galvan proposed a moratorium in August on any new data center development in San Antonio. Since August, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott has also imposed statewide moratoriums on data center projects seeking to connect to the power grid pending audits on their electricity and water use.

“[Microsoft] is proposing to locate in regions of the state that just, from a larger perspective, cannot really handle this level of resource demand,” Shelley says, adding that the state ought to “severely restrict” these facilities’ access to drinkable water. Data centers often use water in cooling systems needed to keep servers from overheating. But the larger part of the facility’s water footprint typically stems from its electricity generation since fossil fuel and nuclear power plants need water for their own cooling systems.

Data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). That’s about 0.4 percent of total water use, but that figure is expected to climb. It’s difficult to predict a precise number because of the uncertainty around which proposed data center projects will ultimately materialize, and what kind of cooling systems they’ll use. But HARC estimates that data centers could consume between 0.5 to 2.7 percent of total annual water use by 2030.

Turning to renewable solar and wind energy can cut down that water use, according to Erin Kinney, manager of coastal resilience and communities and a senior research scientist at HARC. Kinney is also optimistic about the impact Microsoft’s biomimicry projects can have at the local level because the aim is to customize solutions to each location. “I actually think it’s a really exciting concept,” she says. The real test will be in how the company calculates and tracks the benefits and shares that with the local community. “Just as important as making something that fits the ecology, is fitting the community expectations as well,” she said.

Zooming out

Microsoft has a goal of becoming water positive by 2030, meaning it would restore more water than it uses. It similarly has a goal of becoming carbon negative, capturing more planet-heating pollution than it releases by the end of the decade.

Lately, however, the company’s focus on AI has jeopardized some of its sustainability goals. Its carbon pollution jumped 25 percent in 2025, according to its latest sustainability report. And in May, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft is considering abandoning its goal of matching 100 percent of its electricity use with renewable energy on an hourly basis — seen as one of the industry’s most ambitious strategies for encouraging renewable energy growth.

In 2024, after grappling with contradictions she saw between Microsoft’s sustainability goals and the company’s business deals, Holly Alpine left her role leading the company’s ecosystem restoration and climate resilience initiatives in dozens of communities near data centers.

The company’s focus on AI has jeopardized some of its sustainability goals

While she was still at Microsoft, Alpine says, “as a skeptical and extremely passionate climate advocate, I was very excited about the biomimicry projects that I saw, they were extremely well designed to actually provide a positive benefit to the ecosystems where the data center is.” Even so, that was still not enough to outweigh the damage she sees stemming from Microsoft providing cloud services to oil and gas companies and developing AI tools that can be used to optimize fossil fuel production.

She coauthored a research paper published in the journal Nature in August comparing potential AI-driven productivity gains for renewable energy and fossil fuel production, and found that AI ultimately causes more planet-heating emissions than it would help avoid. Big picture, she says, AI is enabling far more pollution than the company is addressing with even well-planned sustainability projects from data center to data center.

“In a period of rapid technological change, we remain focused on advancing our ambition to help address global sustainability challenges across carbon, water, waste, and ecosystems,” Microsoft’s Lyons said in an email to The Verge. “Delivering the infrastructure required to support AI at global scale requires a range of energy solutions in the near term. We continue to invest significantly in carbon free electricity and other decarbonization technologies to reduce emissions across our operations over time.”

The looming question I had for the company was if there was a point where Microsoft would say, “Maybe we just shouldn’t build a data center here” or “This isn’t the right place for this.” To that end, Chuzi was less clear in our interview.

“I think it is an ongoing learning process to understand what that means to be a good neighbor,” Chuzi says. “What it’s going to take to make sure that we are welcome in a community and to earn that place and that part in the community over time.”

articles.body:
Amazon is calling for people to support AI data center projects, or risk irreparable harm to the US economy and national security. In a more than 3,000 word blog posted today, Amazon web services CEO Matt Garman pushed back on public concerns around the impact that data centers may have on jobs, power demands, and the environment, saying “our nation can’t afford to lose” the race for AI dominance.

‘The race our nation can’t afford to lose.’

“With any change, there will be important questions raised, but there will also be misinformation and outright lies, and in the age of social media and 24/7 news, myths take hold faster than ever before,” said Garman. “In fact, this build out is so important geopolitically that there are widespread reports of various countries intentionally seeding misinformation in the US about data centers to trick us into slowing down.”

This comes as support for AI data centers has plummeted in polls, and face increasing backlash from the US communities where they’re being built, with nationwide concerns growing over AI safety and what impact the technology will have on society if left unchecked.

“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” said Garman. “If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations.”

The lengthy memorandum includes a list of practices that Amazon is codifying under a “Data Center Commitment,” around things like creating jobs, preventing increases to local energy rates, and pledging to invest more than $1 billion to support communities that neighbor its data centers. Additionally, Amazon says it no longer uses nondisclosure agreements with government agencies, after Democratic lawmaker Jamie Raskin probed tech companies about the secret deals with local officials.

In an interview about the nondisclosure agreements reported by the The Wall Street Journal, Amazon chief global affairs and legal officer David Zapolsky said “the industry comes from a history of secrecy and so some of that’s just reflex.” He added that community leaders need to share information with their constituents, and that “It just didn’t make sense” to require secrecy anymore.
